edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De resurrectione carnis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.locus: On the Resurrection of the Flesh I
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Fiducia Christianorum, resurrectio mortuorum. Illa credentes sumus; hoc credere veritas cogit. Veritatem Deus aperit; sed vulgus irridet, existimans nihil superesse post mortem; et tamen defunctis parentant, et quidem impensissimo officio, pro moribus eorum, pro temporibus esculentorum; ut quos negant sentire quicquam, escam desiderare praesumant. At ego magis ridebo vulgus, tunc quoque, cum ipsos defunctos atrocissime exurit, quos postmodum gulosissime nutrit, iisdem ignibus et promerens et offendens. O pietatem de crudelitate ludentem! sacrificat, an insultat, cum crematis cremat? Plane cum vulgo interdum et sapientes sententiam suam jungunt. Nihil esse post mortem Epicuri schola est. Ait et Seneca, omnia post mortem finiri, etiam ipsam. Satis est autem, si non minor philosophia Pythagorae et Empedocli. Sed et Platonici immortalem animam e contrario reclamant: imo adhuc proxime etiam in corpora remeabilem affirmant; etsi non in eadem, etsi non in humana tantummodo; ut Euphorbus in Pythagoram, Homerus in pavum recenseantur. Certe recidivatum animae corporalem pronuntiaverunt; tolerabilius mutata, quam negata qualitate: pulsata saltem, licet non adita veritate. Ita saeculum resurrectionem mortuorum, nec cum errat, ignorat.
pass_a_gloss: The confidence of Christians is the resurrection of the dead. We are believers in that; this truth compels us to believe. God reveals the truth; but the crowd ridicules, thinking that nothing remains after death; and yet they pay their respects to the dead, and indeed with a most expensive duty, according to their customs, at the times of feasting; so that they presume that those whom they deny feel anything, desire food. But I will laugh at the crowd even more, then also, when it burns those who have died most cruelly, whom afterwards it feeds most greedily, both earning and offending with the same fires. O piety playing with cruelty! Does it sacrifice, or does it insult, when it burns the cremated? Certainly, even the wise sometimes join their opinion with that of the crowd. The school of Epicurus is that there is nothing after death. Seneca also says that all things, even the soul itself, end after death. But it is enough if not even the philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles is lesser. And yet the Platonists, on the contrary, claim that the soul is immortal; indeed, they even affirm that it is capable of returning into bodies; although not into the same ones, although not only into human ones; so that Euphorbus is said to have been reborn in Pythagoras, and Homer in a peacock. Certainly, they have proclaimed the reincarnation of the soul into a body; more tolerable with a changed quality, than with a denied one: at least struck by, even if not approached by truth. Thus, the age, even when it errs, does not ignore the resurrection of the dead.

pass_b_english: The confidence of Christians rests on the resurrection of the dead. We believe that; truth itself forces us to. God reveals the truth, but the crowd mocks it, convinced nothing survives death—yet they still pay their respects to the dead, and at ruinous expense, following their customs and their feast days. They presume the very people they insist feel nothing are somehow hungry for food. I will laugh at the crowd even harder when it incinerates those same dead with atrocious cruelty, only to turn around and feast them with greedy abandon, using the same fires to both honor and outrage them. O piety playing games with cruelty! Is it sacrifice, or is it insult, to burn the already cremated? Even the wise sometimes align themselves with the crowd's opinion. The Epicurean school teaches there is nothing after death. Seneca says the same: everything ends at death, the soul included. But it is enough if the philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles is not found wanting. The Platonists, by contrast, claim the soul is immortal; indeed, they say it can return to bodies—not the same ones, not only human ones—so that Euphorbus is reborn in Pythagoras, Homer in a peacock. They have proclaimed the soul's reincarnation into a body; a changed existence is more tolerable than a denied one: at least they have been struck by the truth, even if they have not grasped it. Thus the age, even when it errs, does not ignore the resurrection of the dead.

review.notes: Pass A and Pass B both fail to accurately translate the clause 'pulsata saltem, licet non adita veritate'. The Latin 'adita' (from 'adeo', to approach/reach) is rendered in Pass A as 'not approached by truth' and in Pass B as 'not grasped it'. However, the preceding word 'pulsata' (from 'pello', to strike/drive/push) is translated in Pass A as 'at least struck by' and in Pass B as 'at least they have been struck by the truth'. This is a semantic error: 'pulsata' in this context (referring to the soul/reincarnation) means 'touched' or 'buffeted', but the translation 'struck by the truth' implies the truth is the agent hitting them, whereas the Latin structure 'pulsata... licet non adita veritate' suggests the soul is 'touched/buffeted [by the cycle], although not reached by truth'. More critically, Pass A's translation of 'Satis est autem, si non minor philosophia Pythagorae et Empedocli' as 'But it is enough if not even the philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles is lesser' is a failure of logic/syntax; the Latin 'non minor' (not lesser) combined with 'Satis est' (it is enough) is rendered in a way that obscures the comparison. However, the primary failure is the translation of 'pulsata saltem, licet non adita veritate'. In Pass A: 'at least struck by, even if not approached by truth' vs Latin 'pulsata saltem, licet non adita veritate'. The Latin 'adita' is a perfect passive participle. Pass A's 'not approached by truth' is a possible but weak rendering of 'licet non adita veritate'. The most significant error is in Pass A: 'both earning and offending' for 'et promerens et offendens'. 'Promerens' means 'bringing forth/providing/offering up' (in the context of the fires/sacrifices), not 'earning'.
reasons: Pass A translates 'et promerens et offendens' as 'both earning and offending', whereas 'promerens' means 'bringing forth' or 'offering up' (referring to the fires/sacrifices), not 'earning'.

review.notes: The Latin text is correctly translated, with accurate handling of terms like 'fiducia' as 'confidence', 'atrocissime' as 'most cruelly', 'pietatem' as 'piety', and 'saeculum' as 'age'. All citations and content are preserved accurately.
